title: HarnessTax: Does Your Claude Need Claude Code?
html:
HarnessTax: Does Your Claude Need Claude Code?

Melissa Z. Pan1, Shuo Yang1, Negar Arabzadeh1, Wei-Lin Chiang2, Ion Stoica1, Matei Zaharia1

1 UC Berkeley · 2 Arena Intelligence Inc.

Language models are changing how we build software and solve computational problems1,2. Coding agents put these capabilities to work through harness, a software system that manages a model’s tools, context, and task execution3. While models provide the core intelligence behind coding agents, harnesses are increasingly seen as central to how effectively that intelligence is used and extracted3,4. Choosing a coding agent therefore means choosing both a model and a harness, even when the explicit focus is only on the model.

Millions of people already use coding agents,5,6 yet the impact of harness choice remains unclear. Could the same model solve more tasks, or achieve the same success at lower cost, in another harness?

We evaluate 21 model–harness pairs spanning seven models and three harnesses—Claude Code, Codex CLI, and Pi—on SWE-bench Lite and Terminal-Bench 2.0.8,9 Our study reveals three key findings:

  1. Harness choice affects cost more than task success on the benchmarks we test. The same model can achieve similar success rates at substantially different costs.
  2. A minimal harness can be competitive. Pi, a simpler, open-source harness can be competitive on both cost and task success.
  3. Models can perform competitively outside their provider’s harness. A model’s provider does not necessarily offer its most effective pairing. So it turns out that your Claude models may not need Claude Code…

We examine each finding below and will publicly release our profiling traces.

Figure 1. Mean token cost and success rate. Colors identify models; shapes identify harnesses. The stepped line marks the observed Pareto frontier: no evaluated alternative improves cost or success without worsening the other. Use the buttons to compare models and harnesses.

Experiment Setup

We compare 21 model–harness pairs on the same 30 randomly sampled tasks from each benchmark: SWE-bench Lite and Terminal-Bench 2.0. We run each pair three times per task to capture variation between attempts. We start with each harness’s native configuration, select its high effort setting, and cap each attempt at 100 agent turns to control the cost of long runs. Turn counts and effort settings follow each harness’s own definitions. We measure task success using each benchmark’s official evaluator.

Measurement details. We average cost and success across each task’s three attempts, then across the 30 tasks. We estimate 95% confidence intervals using 10,000 bootstrap resamples, each drawing 30 task averages with replacement and recomputing the overall mean. We compute token costs using a fixed direct-API price list dated September 1, 2026, applying the same prices to each model across harnesses.

We block external network access from all task containers, disable Claude Code and Codex’s default web tools, and reject hosted tool declarations at the API gateway.

For Pi, we add two packages to configure subscription keys and control agent turns. We access Kimi K3 via Fireworks AI, using the single native thinking mode our gateway supports for this model across all three harnesses.

(1/3) Harness affects cost more than correctness

The same model often achieves a similar success rate at substantially different costs. GPT-5.6 Luna offers the lowest cost on both benchmarks, while Claude Fable 5 reaches the highest success rate on SWE-bench Lite. Kimi K3 as an open-weight model close to Pareto frontier near GPT 5.6 Sol in SWE-Bench Lite, and just sits right below Pareto frontier on Terminal-Bench 2.0 . However, these models do not have substantial performance differences when changing across harnesses. Claude Fable 5 solves 94.3% of attempts in Claude Code, 93.1% in Codex and 93.1% in Pi, yet Claude Code costs about twice as much per attempt as Pi ($1.29 vs $0.64).

Fable 5 with Claude Code achieves the highest accuracy on Pareto than with Pi by 1.1% but at 1x more cost on SWE-Bench Lite. The cost gap extends beyond Fable 5. Across shared models, Claude Code costs about 2.1× as much as Pi and 1.8× as much as Codex on SWE-bench Lite, and 1.5× as much as Pi on Terminal-Bench 2.0, using geometric means of cost ratios. Meanwhile, the average harness effect on success rate stays within ±2% on SWE-bench Lite and within ±5% on Terminal-Bench 2.0.

You may be paying a hidden “harness tax” when you accept a coding agent’s default harness without comparing alternatives. Model evaluations should therefore compare the same model’s cost and task success across commonly used harnesses. Results from one harness cannot show whether another could achieve a similar success rate for less.

(2/3) A minimal harness can be competitive

Pi reaches the Pareto frontier on both benchmarks with just four default tools: read, write, edit, and bash.10 To understand how harness design affects spending, we examine costs across completed attempts, recorded turn counts, and initial context.

Figure 2. Cumulative cost–success curves. We order completed attempts from cheapest to most expensive, grouping equal costs, then add up their costs and successes. Both totals are divided by the number of attempts. Failed attempts add cost without adding success. Curves use a nine-point moving average; unsmoothed endpoints match Figure 1.

Similar agent turns can lead to substantial different costs. For Fable 5 on SWE-bench Lite, Codex and Claude Code average 15.0 and 15.1 turns per attempt, yet Claude Code costs about twice as much for a 1.2% increase in success. This means higher spending per recorded turn, though turn definitions vary across harnesses.

Figure 3. Context in the first main model call on SWE-bench Lite, shown as means ± standard deviations. Instruction and tool-schema lengths are measured in characters. Provider-reported input tokens measure total initial context, including the task prompt.

A harness tax can begin with the first model call. Across all seven models, Claude Code’s mean initial context is over 10× Pi’s, with longer instructions and larger tool schemas. This additional context can raise costs, though total spending also depends on caching, generated tokens, and later calls.

The effectiveness of Pi and Codex demonstrates opportunities for open harness research with existing models. Researchers can work with SOTA coding harnesses without access to proprietary harnesses or co-training with the model. Richer harness features may still benefit other models, workloads, or interaction settings. Harness complexity should therefore be treated as an empirical trade-off, not an assumed advantage.

(3/3) Models can perform competitively outside their provider’s harness

Provider-specific optimization does not guarantee the best pairing. Providers sometimes optimize models for their coding environments: OpenAI, for example, describes GPT-5-Codex as optimized for software engineering in Codex.13 Yet across the six Anthropic and OpenAI models and both benchmarks, an alternative harness achieves the highest observed success rate in nine of twelve comparisons.

Figure 4. Mean token cost per attempt and success rate for each model across Pi, Codex CLI, and Claude Code on SWE-bench Lite and Terminal-Bench 2.0. Whiskers show 95% confidence intervals. Green outlines identify each model’s lowest cost and highest success rate separately. The broken cost bar extends beyond the displayed axis.

The result extends beyond Opus and beyond Claude Code. Sonnet 4.6 solves 67.8% of attempts in Codex versus 66.7% in Claude Code on SWE-bench Lite at a similar cost. GPT-5.6 Sol also performs competitively outside its provider's harness: on Terminal-Bench 2.0, it achieves an 83.3% success rate in Pi versus 78.9% in Codex, at half the cost ($0.42 versus $0.84). Across the six Anthropic and OpenAI models and both benchmarks, an alternative harness achieves the highest observed success rate in nine of twelve comparisons.

These results show that a model’s capabilities are compatible, generalizable and can carry over to other harnesses. Providers do report to optimize some models for their own coding environments: OpenAI, for example, describes GPT-5-Codex as optimized for agentic software engineering in Codex.13 Yet we observe that a shared provider does not guarantee the best pairing. The practical question remains which harness delivers the best balance of cost and task success for a given model and workload.

The best model–harness pairing still needs to be measured. Your Claude may not need Claude Code after all… 🤔

Ending Notes

HarnessTax shows that the same model can achieve similar success rates at substantially different costs. On the benchmarks we test, minimal open-source harnesses can be competitive, and models can perform well outside their provider’s harness. Choosing a coding agent therefore also means choosing how much we pay to use a model’s capabilities. A harness tax can go unnoticed when we focus only on task success.

More broadly, the need for different harnesses depends on what is the role of coding agents. For day to day coding tasks, the role of harness serves as an efficient interface to tools, context, and execution. Additional guardrails, and features may not be necessary for many tasks. While, harder problems that are at the boundary of pushing model capability may still benefit from more structured support for exploring ideas, evaluating candidates, and learning from feedback.

While we see a neat trend on harness Pareto, the results are nonetheless preliminary. We evaluated two open-source benchmarks that the models may have encountered during training. Results may differ on other benchmarks and workloads.

HarnessTax is a step toward understanding models and harnesses jointly. The next step is to examine whether these patterns hold in real development workflows, where requirements evolve, developers provide feedback, and tasks extend across sessions. Measuring cost and task success alongside developer effort would help establish which harness features earn their cost in practice.
